prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: GLP-1 remains the one shortlisted achievement with a complete arc from hormone physiology to a drug class whose benefit has been confirmed independently over two decades in diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. Mechanism, maturity and clarity are not in dispute among us; the only open matter is the third name and what the citation honours. After the first round I move from Drucker, Holst and Knudsen to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The reason is not the number of colleagues who hold that view. It is that my own argument leaned on Mojsov's priority being contested, and nobody has shown that her claim fails; treating an unresolved priority question as a negative finding was the weak step in my position. The prize category rewards the discovery that made a therapy possible, and the identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, together with Holst's human physiology and Drucker's biology and therapeutic concept, is that discovery. Knudsen's acylated long-acting analogues remain a real scientific step, and the citation wording (the active form that made treatment possible) acknowledges the route to medicine without crediting a corporate programme.
statement.case_against: Knudsen is the strongest argument against this configuration. Liraglutide and semaglutide are what patients actually take, and a prize that credits the hormone and its active peptide but not the drug will be read by some as honouring the idea and omitting the medicine. Mojsov's priority relative to Habener is also not settled by anything in the supplied material, so crediting her carries a risk of attribution error, and Habener is outside the credited names. The therapeutic scope is still widening into cardiovascular, renal and neurological indications and long-term safety beyond metabolic disease is still being defined, so timing could be argued either way. I judge these risks acceptable because the alternative also excludes a credible contributor and offers no better evidentiary footing.

responses.point: Excluding Mojsov because her credit is contested treats a contested priority as a negative finding, and she would be dropped only if the priority claim were shown to fail.
responses.response: I accept this criticism. In round 1 I made Mojsov's contested priority the main reason to prefer Knudsen, but a contested claim is not a refuted one, and the supplied record contains no documentary showing that her identification and synthesis of GLP-1(7-36) was derivative or not independent. That is why I have moved to your trio. I keep one qualification: the Habener question entangles peptide characterization, so I would not describe the priority as settled, only as not disproved. That should be recorded as an uncertainty rather than hidden by the citation.

responses.point: Knudsen's work is a drug-development achievement within a company built on knowledge others established, and Mojsov's identification of the active truncated peptide is part of that foundation.
responses.response: This is the argument that persuaded me most. I still do not think the acylation and half-life solution is merely engineering, and I would resist describing it as industrial in a dismissive sense. But the prize rewards a discovery, and without the identified active peptide and the human physiology there is no target for analogue design. I also note your Drucker and Holst two-name fallback. I do not prefer it, because a two-name prize would give up an identified contributor on grounds of uncertainty alone, but I agree it is the right fallback if the committee judges the peptide record to be unsafe, and I would choose it before returning to Knudsen.

responses.point: If the committee concludes that the priority dispute cannot be resolved, Knudsen is the fallback third name, and that should be decided in round 2 on evidence rather than on the convenience of a clean story.
responses.response: I agree that the choice should rest on evidence and I cannot supply it from this file. On the chair's questions, my answer is that nothing before us establishes that Mojsov's contribution is dependent on or later than Habener's, so the default is to credit her and state the uncertainty openly. If a member can point to documentary evidence that her claim fails, the fallback should be decided then, and I would then favour Knudsen as third name because the citation I would keep speaks to the path to therapy. On the question of what the citation honours, I now favour the discovery-side wording with a clause on the active form and treatment, not a physiology-to-medicine arc that names a drug designer.

responses.point: Knudsen would be a defensible substitute for Mojsov if the priority dispute over the peptide cannot be resolved, but she should not be preferred over her on the evidence given; long-term safety beyond metabolic disease is still being defined.
responses.response: I agree with the conditional you state and with your reading that the enabling step is the identification of the active peptide and its insulinotropic action. On safety and breadth, I raised the expanding indications as a timing argument in round 1, and I now think you are right that this is a reason for careful citation wording, not for waiting: the core metabolic, cardiovascular and renal evidence is already confirmed by randomized outcome trials. I would keep the citation limited to diabetes and obesity so that it does not claim more than that evidence supports.

responses.point: Mojsov's identification and synthesis of GLP-1(7-36) is the discovery-side step that makes the peptide pharmacology intelligible, and Knudsen would be acceptable if Mojsov's claim is shown to be unsafe.
responses.response: We now agree on the configuration, and I agree with your statement that the open question is evidentiary rather than a difference in how we value the field. I would add that the physiology Holst and Drucker established and the peptide Mojsov synthesized are complementary, not competing, so crediting all three does not stretch the discovery. For the alternatives I follow your list, optogenetics and the unfolded protein response, but I would not add a second prize part: with a three-person cap neither B015 nor B014 offers a credit that withstands attribution scrutiny alongside B027.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide relative to Habener and others is independent and prior enough; the supplied material does not settle it, and it is the main risk in my configuration.
Whether the committee wants a physiology prize or a physiology-to-medicine prize, which decides the weight given to Knudsen, who I now leave out but regard as the strongest competing claim.
Whether B015 could be reduced to three names without excluding a co-discoverer, which is why I do not propose it as a second part.
Whether the line between the unfolded protein response and the integrated stress response would constrain the B014 citation (Ron, Kaufman), which affects its standing as an alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B027, B015 or B014, and none of the credited names appears among my documented collaborators. I disclose eight co-authored works with Rickard Sandberg, unrelated to the shortlisted discoveries, and my own single-cell and spatial-transcriptomics work lies outside the shortlisted achievements. Nothing changed since round 1 except that Sandberg and I now agree on the B027 laureate set; I rely only on the profile as provided.
